claims.statement: Loong belongs to Chinese mythology and commonly has a serpentine shape with four legs.
claims.statement_id: Loong adalah naga dalam mitologi Tiongkok, lazim digambarkan menyerupai ular dengan empat kaki.
claims.quote: The Chinese dragon, known as long or loong (/lʊŋ/ LUUNG) is a legendary creature in Chinese mythology, Chinese folklore, and Chinese culture generally. Chinese dragons have many animal-like forms, such as turtles and fish, but are most commonly depicted as snake-like with four legs.

claims.statement: The dragon served as an emblem of imperial authority in Chinese history.
claims.statement_id: Naga menjadi lambang kekuasaan kaisar dalam sejarah Tiongkok.
claims.quote: Historically, the Chinese dragon was associated with the emperor of China and used as a symbol to represent imperial power. Liu Bang, the founder of the Han dynasty, claimed that he was conceived after his mother dreamt of a dragon. During the Tang dynasty, emperors wore robes with dragon motif as an imperial symbol, and high officials might also be presented with dragon robes.

claims.statement: Coiled dragon forms occur on jade amulets from the Shang period.
claims.statement_id: Bentuk naga melingkar juga ditemukan pada amulet giok zaman Shang.
claims.quote: The coiled dragon or snake form played an important role in early Chinese culture. The character for "dragon" in the earliest Chinese writing has a similar coiled form, as do later jade dragon amulets from the Shang period.

claims.statement: Scientific examination identifies many objects called dragon bones as mammal fossils.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian benda yang dahulu disebut tulang naga ternyata fosil mamalia.
claims.quote: Scientific examination of "dragon bones" from the 19th century to the present suggests they most commonly are remains of fossil Cenozoic mammals, such as the extinct horse Hipparion.

claims.statement: Wang Fu recorded a tradition of nine animal resemblances in dragon anatomy.
claims.statement_id: Wang Fu mencatat tradisi sembilan kemiripan anatomi naga dengan hewan lain.
claims.quote: From its origins as totems or the stylized depiction of natural creatures, the Chinese dragon evolved to become a mythical animal. The Han dynasty scholar Wang Fu recorded Chinese myths that long dragons had nine anatomical resemblances.

claims.statement: Doré records an anatomical variant with deer antlers and a crocodile head.
claims.statement_id: Doré mencatat varian anatomi dengan tanduk rusa dan kepala buaya.
claims.quote: "The antlers of a deer. The head of a crocodile. A demon's eyes. The neck of a snake. A tortoise's viscera. A hawk's claws. The palms of a tiger. A cow's ears. And it hears through its horns, its ears being deprived of all power of hearing".

claims.statement: Art often shows dragons pursuing or contesting a flaming pearl.
claims.statement_id: Naga dalam seni sering mengejar atau memperebutkan mutiara menyala.
claims.quote: Many pictures of Chinese dragons show a flaming pearl under their chin or in their claws. The pearl is associated with spiritual energy, wisdom, prosperity, power, immortality, thunder, or the moon. Chinese art often depicts a pair of dragons chasing or fighting over a flaming pearl.

claims.statement: Popular belief connects dragons with rivers, seas, and the distribution of rain.
claims.statement_id: Kepercayaan populer menghubungkan naga dengan sungai, laut, dan pengaturan hujan.
claims.quote: Chinese dragons are strongly associated with water and weather in popular religion. They are believed to be the rulers of moving bodies of water, such as waterfalls, rivers, or seas. The Dragon god is the dispenser of rain as well as the zoomorphic representation of yang, the masculine power of generation.

claims.statement: During drought or flooding, villagers offered sacrifices and religious rites to appease local dragon kings and seek rain.
claims.statement_id: Saat kekeringan atau banjir, masyarakat melakukan ritual untuk memohon bantuan raja naga setempat.
claims.quote: Because of this association, they are seen as "in charge" of water-related weather phenomena. In premodern times, many Chinese villages (especially those close to rivers and seas) had temples dedicated to their local "dragon king".

claims.statement: One legend describes the Yellow Emperor ascending to heaven after becoming a dragon.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah legenda mengisahkan Kaisar Kuning naik ke langit setelah menjadi naga.
claims.quote: According to Chinese legend, both Chinese primogenitors, the earliest Door and the Yellow Emperor, were closely related to the dragon. At the end of his reign, the first legendary ruler, the Yellow Emperor, was said to have been immortalized into a dragon that resembled his emblem, and ascended to Heaven.

claims.statement: The Norton Museum describes dragons as heavenly rulers petitioned for rain through ritual.
claims.statement_id: Museum Norton menjelaskan naga sebagai penguasa langit yang dimohon mendatangkan hujan dalam ritual.
claims.quote: Each work depicts dragons, the heavenly sovereigns, petitioned to bring rain in ritual ceremonies.

claims.statement: On court robes, dragon imagery refers to the emperor’s mandate to rule from the Dragon Throne.
claims.statement_id: Pada jubah istana, naga merujuk pada mandat kaisar untuk memerintah dari Takhta Naga.
claims.quote: The presence of dragons on the robes refers to the emperor holding the Mandate of Heaven to rule from the Dragon Throne.

claims.quote: It is highly unlikely the decorator of this object knew that the image depicts the Chinese legend of the Dragon pursuing the ‘Flaming Pearl’ representing wisdom, enlightenment and spiritual essence.

claims.statement: Dragon patterns on Chinese export ceramics inspired British printed blue-and-white wares in the nineteenth century.

claims.quote: Nüwa, also read Nügua, is a mother goddess, culture hero, and/or member of the Three Sovereigns of Chinese mythology. She is a goddess in Chinese folk religion, Chinese Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism. She is credited with creating humanity and repairing the Pillar of Heaven.

claims.statement: A creation account describes her shaping people from yellow clay.
claims.statement_id: Kisah penciptaan menggambarkannya membentuk manusia dengan tanah liat kuning.
claims.quote: As creator of mankind, she molded humans individually by hand with yellow clay. In other stories where she fulfills this role, she only created nobles and/or the rich out of yellow soil. The stories vary on the other details about humanity's creation, but it was a tradition commonly believed in ancient China that she created commoners from brown mud.

claims.statement: Another version distinguishes hand-shaped people from those made using a muddy cord.

claims.quote: A story holds that she was tired when she created "the rich and the noble", so all others, or "cord-made people", were created from her "dragg[ing] a string through mud".

claims.quote: A nian beast (traditional Chinese: 年獸; simplified Chinese: 年兽; Hanyu Pinyin: Nián shòu; Tongyong Pinyin: Nián shòu; Wade–Giles: Nien2 shou4; Cantonese Yale: Nìhn sau; Zhuyin Fuhao: ㄋㄧㄢˊ ㄕㄡˋ) is a beast in Chinese mythology. According to Chinese mythology, the nian lives under the sea or in the mountains. The Chinese character nian more usually means "year" or "new year".

claims.statement: The earliest written sources describing Nian as a creature date from the early 20th century.
claims.statement_id: Catatan tertulis tentang Nian sebagai makhluk baru diketahui dari awal abad kedua puluh.
claims.quote: The earliest written sources that refer to the nian as a creature date to the early 20th century.

claims.statement: The tale describes it emerging at New Year to feed on people and animals.
claims.statement_id: Kisah menyebutnya keluar pada tahun baru untuk memangsa manusia dan hewan.
claims.quote: Once every year at the beginning of Chinese New Year, the nian would come out of its hiding place to feed, mostly on people and animals. During the winter, when food was scarce, it would raid villages, eating the crops and sometimes the villagers themselves - particularly their children.

claims.statement: Nian's appearance varies, including a flat-faced lion with a dog's body.
claims.statement_id: Penampilan Nian memiliki varian, termasuk singa berwajah datar dengan tubuh anjing.
claims.quote: Several accounts describe its appearance, with some claiming that it resembles a flat-faced lion with the body of a dog and prominent incisors.

claims.statement: A legend explains red lanterns as an attempt to avert Nian's attacks.
claims.statement_id: Legenda menjelaskan pemasangan lentera merah sebagai upaya menghindari serangan Nian.
claims.quote: Some local legends attribute the Chinese lion dance (舞獅) to the nian. The tradition has its origins in a story of a nian's attack on a village. After the attack, the villagers discussed how to make the nian leave them in peace. Since it was discovered that the beast was afraid of the color red, people put red lanterns and spring scrolls on their windows and doors.

claims.statement: Celebration practices were recorded in ancient texts without mentioning a creature named Nian.
claims.statement_id: Praktik perayaan lebih dahulu tercatat dalam teks kuno tanpa menyebut makhluk bernama Nian.
claims.quote: Various aspects of cultural practices relating to Chinese New Year are part of the nian legend. These cultural practices are recorded in ancient texts, though none of them refer to a creature called nian.

claims.quote: He is thought to have been an influence on the later half-dragon, half-turtle figure of Bixi in imperial Chinese sculpture. Bixi was considered a son of the Dragon King who was able to carry enormous weights upon his back; figures of the dragon-turtle bearing memorial stelae are common monuments throughout East Asia.

claims.statement: Gwisin are spirits of dead people in Korean folklore, distinct from dokkaebi.
claims.statement_id: Gwisin adalah roh orang mati dalam cerita rakyat Korea, berbeda dari dokkaebi.
claims.quote: In Korean folklore, Gwisin (Korean: 귀신) are a type of deity, divinity, spirit or ghost. They are considered similar to a yogoe (Korean: 요괴) or mamul (Korean: 마물). Unlike dokkaebi, gwisin are humans who have died.

claims.statement: Ties to the living, such as revenge or care for loved ones, may keep a spirit on earth.
claims.statement_id: Ikatan dengan dunia hidup, seperti balas dendam atau menjaga orang tersayang, dapat menahan roh di bumi.
claims.quote: According to folklore, gwisin may be found in many places. It is claimed that when an individual dies but still has ties to the world of the living, such as in the case of revenge or caring for a loved one, their spirit remains on earth to complete the task before going on to the underworld.

claims.statement: Revenge is a common theme in gwisin tales.
claims.statement_id: Balas dendam menjadi tema umum cerita tentang gwisin.
claims.quote: There are a lot of legends about gwisin. Because they are a common form of ghost, children often make them up to scare others or parents tell stories to their children to teach them a lesson. The most common plot of a legend about gwisin is revenge, for example revenge for the family of the ghost. Another popular trope includes men who cheat on their wives, and murder someone.

claims.statement: Cheonyeo-gwisin is the spirit of a woman who died unmarried.

claims.quote: The Cheonyeo-gwisin (처녀귀신) is the gwisin of a woman who died unmarried and usually have white Hanbok (한복) which are worn for funerals.

claims.statement: Mul-gwisin is the spirit of a drowned person.

claims.quote: The Mul-gwisin (물귀신) is the spirit of someone who drowned.

claims.statement: The Four Holy Beasts are a group of Chinese auspicious creatures mentioned in the Book of Rites.
claims.statement_id: Four Holy Beasts adalah kelompok makhluk bertuah Tiongkok yang disebut dalam Kitab Ritus.
claims.quote: The Four Holy Beasts (Chinese: 四靈、四聖獸、or 四大神獸) are Chinese astronomical and cultural Four Benevolent Animals that are spread in the East Asian cultural sphere. They are mentioned in the Chinese classic Book of Rites and includes the Dragon (龍) in the East, the Qilin (麟) in the West, the Turtle (龜) in the North, and the Fenghuang (鳳) in the South.

claims.quote: The Four Holy Beasts differs from  Four Symbols in that Qilin replaces the White Tiger.  The Four Symbols are the Azure Dragon (青龍) in the East, White Tiger (白虎) in the West, Vermilion Bird (朱雀) in the South, and the Black Turtle-Snake (玄武) in the North.
